topic: What if you never sleep again?
title: WHAT IF YOU NEVER
SLEPT AGAIN?

power.rule: every skipped hour fills a clock above your bed, and someone else loses that sleep
power.look: a glass clock over the bed fills with blue light, then turns red as the debt compounds

script.beat: 1 cold open: three demos, then the word
script.text: Alarm screams. You smile. Bank. Eight hours in the glass. Quiz paper drops. Every answer clicks. Bank. Your little sister asks for a story. You don't yawn. She does. Bank.
What if you never slept again? Every hour you skip flows into the clock above your bed. But sleep can't be made. It has to come from someone.

First week, you're a machine. Homework at midnight. Your mum's car fixed by breakfast. Mo beaten at every game. You write a song on the bus. You read every page twice. The glass clock glows. Sixteen hours. Twenty. Twenty-four. The city sleeps. You don't.

script.beat: 4 the turn: the cost, with one real number
script.text: Then the debt comes due. Six hours or less a night for two weeks left people as impaired as two entire nights awake. That's real. Your focus doesn't fade. It compounds. You smile at the wrong name. You miss the last step. Microsleeps blink through your eyes. A red light becomes a memory. Your hands forget the turn.
The sleep clinic sees it. A suit with a clipboard watches the clock, not you. Every hour in the glass is an hour stolen from a name on his list. Mo is on it. Then your sister. Then your mum.

Tonight the clock holds forty hours. Enough to win tomorrow. Enough to stay awake forever. The suit offers one deal. Pour it back, and lose the week. Keep it, and your sister never dreams again. Your mum drives the night shift. Mo waits in the dark. The clock ticks louder.
You reach for the clock. It reaches back. Part one.

science.claim: Six hours or less a night for two weeks left people as impaired as two entire nights awake.
science.working: Van Dongen et al. tested chronic sleep restriction and report deficits equivalent to up to two nights of total sleep deprivation in the six-hour-or-less group. Extra wakefulness above a 15.84 h baseline over 14 nights is about 58 h, close to the 48 h comparator, so the claim follows the source without rounding up the effect.
science.source: Van Dongen et al., Sleep 2003, 26(2):117-126, https://academic.oup.com/sleep/article/26/2/117/2709164; U.S. DoD 2021 sleep-deprivation readiness report

science.claim: Microsleeps are brief losses of consciousness lasting four or five seconds.
science.working: CDC/NIOSH describes microsleeps as brief losses of consciousness lasting four or five seconds. At 55 mph, 24.4 m/s multiplied by 4-5 s gives 98-122 m, about 107-133 yards of travel.
